Introduction:
Asbestos has been extensively used in industry for over a century due to its properties. Its harmful pulmonary effects, including asbestosis, were recognized in the early 1900s and, in 1973, the International Agency for Research on Cancer classified all types of asbestos as carcinogenic, a designation confirmed in 2012 [ 1 , 2 ].

Despite the well-established link between asbestos exposure and several cancers, including mesothelioma, only 72 countries had banned all forms of asbestos by early 2025 [ 3 ]. Italy—historically one of the largest consumers—implemented a national ban in 1992 (Law 257/92).

Mesothelioma incidence and mortality at the small-area level (i.e. municipality or census tract) are widely accepted as indicators of asbestos exposure, considering the high etiological fraction due to asbestos (>80% of cases) and the poor prognosis (at the population level in Italy, 50% of the patients survive for <10 months from diagnosis) [ 4–7 ]. Mesothelioma has a long latency (30–50 years since the first asbestos exposure) and affects the pleura in ∼90% of cases, even if other anatomic sites could be affected (i.e. peritoneum, pericardium, vaginal tunic of testis). While occupational exposure remains the primary source of risk, environmental and domestic exposures also contribute.

Since the 1980s, a national epidemiological surveillance plan monitoring mortality from mesothelioma has been updated in Italy. Despite the ban, high mortality persists: between 2010 and 2016, ∼4400 people per year died from asbestos-related diseases and, in the 2010–20 period, an average of 1545 people per year died from mesothelioma (3.79 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants, 35% of all asbestos-related diseases), making Italy one of the most severely impacted countries [ 7 , 8 ]. The latest report from the National Registry of Mesothelioma, which has been operating at the national level since 2003, estimated in Italy a total of 37 003 mesothelioma diagnoses between 1993 and 2021 [ 6 ].

This study aims to contribute to the national surveillance plan for mesothelioma by analysing the mortality trends for pleural mesothelioma (PM) in Italy over 40 years (1980–2020), focusing on calendar periods and birth cohorts. Furthermore, relative risks (RRs) are modelled in space and time by using hierarchical Bayesian methods. We analysed PM because it makes up a high proportion of all mesothelioma (>90%) and there was no specific nosological code before 2003.
Methods:
### Mortality data

Data on deaths caused by pleural malignant tumours [International Classification of Diseases, 9th edition (ICD-9): 163] and PM [International Classification of Diseases, 10th edition (ICD-10): C45.0] were extracted by using the Statistical Service of the Italian National Institute of Health from the National Mortality Database of the National Census Bureau (ISTAT) for the period 1980–2020, at both the national and regional levels, and separately for the sex assigned at birth. For the period from 1995 (the year in which the multiple-cause-of-death registries became available) to 2002 (the last year in which the ICD-9 classification was in force), we used two sources of data: the multiple-cause-of-death registries and the National Mortality Database, both maintained by ISTAT. The multiple-cause-of-death registries are single, anonymous electronic registries that contain all the causes of death exactly as typed in full by the coroner on the death certificate. To identify the cause of death of the 8508 classified people who died with code 163.9 ‘Malignant neoplasm of pleura, unspecified’, we examined individual entries in the database of multiple causes of death and we identified all people for whom the term ‘mesothelioma’ and the term ‘pleura’ were written as the underlying cause. We obtained information on 6242 people who died with PM. We then used the same proportion of mesothelioma out of the total number of pleural cancers observed in 1995 to adjust for previous years back to 1980.

The data were grouped into 18 5-year age classes (0–4 to 85+ years) and 8 calendar periods (1980–4, …, 2015–20). Over time, we followed 15 birth cohorts (1905–14, …, 1975–84), highlighted in the Lexis diagram ( Supplementary Table 1 ).

### Descriptive analyses

We performed descriptive analyses on the calendar period, evaluating direct standardized rates (using the 2013 European standard population as the reference) and standardized mortality ratios (SMRs, using the Italian population of 1980–2020 as the reference) for PM. We computed cumulative risks and SMRs for people aged 20–84 years by using the 1935–44 birth cohort as the reference. For the computational details, refer to the Supplementary Material .

Age-period-cohort (APC) models were fitted to national data to estimate the adjusted mortality rate ratios for calendar periods and birth cohorts, and the model fit was assessed by using deviance and Pearson chi-square statistics.

### Space-cohort Bayesian model

We modelled PM mortality risk across Italian regions and birth cohorts by using hierarchical Bayesian models with structured random effects for space and time, following Knorr–Held’s approach [ 9 ]. The death counts in each region ( i = 1, …, 20) and cohort ( j = 1905–14 to 1960–9) were assumed to follow a Poisson distribution with mean E i j θ i j ⁠ , where E i j represents the number of expected cases (calculated by using as reference the 1935–44 birth cohort) and θ i j denotes the RR.

We assumed both the spatial and temporal structures for the interaction term [ 9 ].

We used WinBUGS32 to perform the Monte Carlo Markov chain analyses and STATA18 (StataCorp LP, College Station, TX) for statistical analyses.
Results:
In Italy, between 1980 and 2020, a total of 40 702 people died from malignant tumours of the pleura (28 117 males and 12 585 females); of these—after correction for the absence of a specific ICD-9 code for PM—35 134 had PM (24 380 males and 10 754 females), averaging 878 deaths per year. In Table 1 , we report previous adjusted estimates, ICD-9 codes for malignant pleural tumours, and our adjusted estimates (see ‘Methods’ section) [ 12 ]. The last observation period of 2015–20 registered the highest number of deaths.

Table 2 presents the absolute number of deaths and age-specific rates (per 100 000 individuals) by calendar period, stratified by sex. The age group with the highest mortality was 75–79 years, with 4716 deaths among males and 2089 among females during the entire period. The male/female ratio over the whole observation period was 2.27.

These rates seemed to be decreasing, or in some cases reaching a plateau, in the last periods for age classes of between 50 and 75 years. The same rates are plotted by calendar periods and birth cohorts in Fig. 1 (graphs are reported on a logarithmic scale in Supplementary Figure 1 ). The direct standardized rates for males, displayed in Fig. 2 (dark red represents males, sand represents females) alongside SMRs, showed a stable increase until 2014, reaching a plateau in the last period of observation, with a slight decrease. This trend was not as evident for the female population. The increase for males was also consistent with the calendar-period SMR, reaching a peak again in the period of 2010–14. Females experienced a less linear trend, with higher ratios than males until 1999. Nonetheless, their SMR was still above the national standard at the end of the observation period. The analysis by birth cohort, represented here by the cumulative SMR, showed that the most affected cohorts were born between 1935 and 1949 for both males and females. Indeed, the two increasing trends differed: although females reached lower SMR values, they remained above the reference level among the younger cohorts. For cohorts born after the peak, a clear and consistent decrease was observed for both sexes. These same figures are reported for the specific regional profiles of the most affected regions (Friuli-Venezia Giulia, Liguria, Lombardy, Piedmont) in the Supplementary Material ( Supplementary Figures 2–5 ).

Fig. 3 shows the regional profiles for males and females of the RRs obtained from the spatio-temporal model for each birth cohort from the first in 1905–14 to the one in 1960–69. The cohorts after 1960–69 were excluded as too few cases were observed. The region with the highest risk for males was Liguria, with an RR of 3.22 (95% credibility interval: 2.98, 3.52), followed by Friuli-Venezia Giulia, with 2.27 (95% credibility interval: 1.96, 2.61). Notably, these regions reached their risk peaks in different cohorts: 1935–44 for Liguria and 1940–9 for Friuli-Venezia Giulia. The Piedmont region exhibited the highest risk among females, with an RR of 2.45 (95% credibility interval: 2.16, 2.76), followed by Lombardy, with 1.82 (95% credibility interval: 1.66, 1.98), and Liguria, with 1.80 (95% credibility interval: 1.56, 2.06). Both sexes exhibited an increasing trend, reaching their peaks in the cohorts between 1935 and 1949, as observed from the cumulative SMR, with some regional differences. Supplementary Table 3 reports the RRs for each region stratified by birth cohort and sex.

Fig. 4 presents maps of the RR distribution obtained from the spatio-temporal model for males and females. A well-known north–south gradient was evident, with the northern regions consistently showing higher risks than the southern ones. Among all areas, only Liguria exhibited consistently elevated risks in the youngest birth cohorts for both males and females. Maps of the regional SMRs and the posterior probabilities P (RR > 1) are reported in Supplementary Figures 6 and 7 .
Discussion:
We analysed 40 years of PM mortality data in Italy, enabling risk assessment by birth cohort (1905–84).

Our results update previous investigations estimating a decreasing risk of mortality in male cohorts born after 1945 in Italy [ 13 , 14 ].

In absolute terms, in Italy, the burden of mortality for PM was relevant, summing to 35 134 deaths between 1980 and 2020. The birth cohorts contributing more were those in 1935–49. We confirm previous observations of a higher risk of PM among women compared with those in other countries [ 6 , 8 ]. Women’s asbestos exposures, in our country, were reported mainly in the context of textile [ 6 , 15 , 16 ], domestic (i.e. wives of asbestos-cement workers), and environmental settings [ 6 , 8 , 17–19 ].

Asbestos was banned in 1992, contributing to the decrease in occupational exposure that dated back to the late 1970s, as shown by the risk profile of the birth cohorts [ 20 ].

Indeed, trends in the mortality of asbestos-related diseases by birth cohort reflect almost perfectly those of asbestos consumption, with a lag that is roughly proportional to the latency period. People born between 1935 and 1949 in Italy entered the workforce approximately two to three decades later, between 1955 and 1980—a period during which Italy was among the major asbestos producers and users in Europe (our country reached the peak of consumption in 1980, at >180 000 metric tons) [ 3 ].

There were 7 cases in males and 13 in females below ages 20–24 vs 10 years in the pre-asbestos-ban periods (see Table 2 ) [ 6 , 8 ]. PM in young people could have been due to domestic and/or environmental asbestos exposures since their early-life years [ 4 ]. However, in the literature, asbestos exposure was documented in <5% of paediatric mesothelioma [ 21 ]. Misclassification cannot be excluded, as we were able to use death certificate descriptions from 1995 onward to adjust the ICD-9 codes for pleural tumours. We have no explanation for the gender difference.

We cannot exclude an effect of improved survival on the decrease in mortality in the more recent decade. However, access to modern treatments would have resulted in a significant period effect in APC modelling, but we did not find evidence of that. Also, improved median survival was up to <20 months—a time that is too short to have caused differences in the data aggregated in 5-year classes [ 22 ].

The trend in Italy appeared similar to those in other Western countries that have banned asbestos, with the highest risks in individuals who lived or started working before the total ban. Northern European countries—where the first restrictions on asbestos use began in the mid-1970s and total bans were implemented in the early 1980s (except in Finland, where the ban occurred in 1992)—showed a peak in PM risk for the birth cohorts of 1937–47 corresponding to occupational histories aligning with the peak of asbestos use (1960–75) [ 23 ]. A similar figure was observed in the UK, where the use of blue and brown asbestos was banned in 1985 [ 24 ]. In Spain, where asbestos was banned more recently (2002), an increasing risk of mortality from pleural cancers was observed, rising to a maximum in the 1944–8 birth cohorts [ 25 ]. In the USA, an analysis based on nine cancer registries showed a peak of PM risk for the 1921–30 birth cohorts [ 26 ]. All studies agree that mesothelioma risk trends reflect asbestos consumption, which peaked around World War II and the post-war reconstruction in the USA and in the 1970s in industrialized European countries [ 13 , 26 ].

One of the most interesting aspects of our work relies on specific regional analyses. We found a strong heterogeneity among Italian regions that was consistent with historical patterns of asbestos exposure within Italy. For males, Liguria emerged as the region with the highest risk values, reaching its maximum for the earlier birth cohort. Liguria has a long history of shipbuilding—e.g. in the navy and military arsenal in La Spezia and with the navy and steel industry in Genoa—which dates back to the period from the end of the nineteenth century to the beginning of the twentieth century, with an important phase in the post-war period. Similar figures apply to Friuli-Venezia Giulia, which showed the second-highest risks for males and is home to well-known shipbuilding and naval engineering [ 6 ]. Lombardy and Piedmont follow and showed a birth-cohort curve of RRs for PM that peaked later than those of the previous regions of Liguria and Friuli-Venezia Giulia. Several investigations reported the high risk of asbestos exposure in these regions, particularly corresponding to former asbestos-cement plants (Broni in Lombardy and Casale Monferrato in Piedmont) and the largest European chrysotile mine (Balangero, Piedmont) [ 6 , 8 , 16 , 17 , 27 ].

For females, the situation differed due to distinct exposure patterns compared with males. An exceeding risk was observed in Liguria for older birth cohorts, and in Piedmont and Lombardy, where females were frequently employed in textile factories—one of the work sectors most involved in asbestos-exposure risks [ 6 , 15 ]—and domestic and environmental exposures in the female population were reported in the areas in which asbestos-cement plants were located [ 18 , 19 ]. Moreover, elevated risk in females was observed in Aosta Valley, where two mines of chrysotile and tremolite were active, and potential environmental exposure to asbestos-bearing rocks was reported [ 6 , 28 ].

In the literature, we found a description of spatio-temporal patterns of PM risk for a few regions only, mostly based on incidence data from local cancer registries [ 29 , 30 ].

Fine-scale spatial analysis could have been affected by misclassification, as the residence at death may not have reflected where the exposure was suffered, due to migration after retirement. In contrast, the method used for the estimates of PM mortality before the ICD-10 code, based on multiple-cause-of-death, is more accurate than earlier methods [ 31 ].

These findings, showing in Italy a persistent mesothelioma mortality risk, even if decreasing in young generations, underscore the need to address the legacy of asbestos exposure and to trace new exposure contexts in Italy. Cohort-based surveillance, highlighting the subpopulations with higher risk, is critical for public health planning and compensation schemes, and can serve as a model for countries in which asbestos is still used. Coordinated action is essential to ensure environmental justice and global efforts towards a world ban.
